newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania to end currency board, keep dollar peg.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania to end currency board, keep dollar peg.

text.p: Lithuania's central bank on Thursday said it would take steps to end the currency board system of regulating the country's litas currency but would keep the litas pegged at four to one dollar.
The Bank of Lithuania central bank said that the bank's board discussed and in essence approved its programme to scrap the currency board and regain all the powers of a central bank.
But the central bank said in a statement that the link to the dollar would be maintained without the currency board.
The bank said that its new programme had three stages.
"The currency rate policy will not be changed, neither during the first stage nor during the second stage," the bank said. "The litas peg to the dollar will be firmly preserved."
A bank spokeswoman said the programme would be further discussed in detail next Thursday.
The main tenet of the currency board is that hard currency reserves have to back the amount of local currency in circulation at the fixed exchange rate.
This prevents governments from printing money that it cannot back, but strips the central bank of powers to influence monetary policy or market conditions.
In the first stage, the bank would begin to assume some powers to influence the liquidity of the banking market with repurchase auctions of government Treasury bills.
During this stage, the currency board would operate unchanged.
But the second stage of the process would involve the gradual end of the currency board, still keeping the currency peg.
The third stage, which would start no sooner than 1998, involved a process to bring the litas closer to the planned European currency, the euro.

This stage would involve a transition period when the litas could be pegged to both the U.S. dollar and the German mark. If the currency policy is changed after 1999, the peg would be made to the U.S. dollar and the euro.
Lithuania has applied for European Union membership and wants to integrate more closely with the West.
